name: Greek
confidence_why: Revithiadou (1999), van Oostendorp (2012), Revithiadou, Nikolou and Papadopoulou (2015), Revithiadou and colleagues (2026) and Joseph (2006) all describe Modern Greek stress as lexically and morphologically specified, unpredictable from syllable weight and confined to the last three syllables of the word, and the only point on which they differ is which syllable serves as the default when no morpheme carries its own stress.

catalog_quote: Greek syllable structure lacks distinctions of phonological weight; all syllables are of equal phonological weight (Joseph and Philippaki 1987). Greek is a bounded system; the scope of primary stress is limited to the last three syllables of the word. Feet in Greek are trochaic. ... Morphologically equivalent words such as án7ropos 'man', fantáros 'soldier' and uranós 'sky', for instance, exhibit phonologically unmotivated differences in stress. The complexity of the system is further enhanced by accentual alternations that take place within the paradigm as in án7ropos (NOM.sg), an7rópu (GEN.sg). ... the best way to analyze stress in nouns and adjectives is to assume that the respective morphemes are inherently marked. Lexical accents mark one of the last three positions of the word because Greek is a three-syllable-window language. For example, stress is on the antepenult in án7ropos, …

new_statements.quote: There is consensus that stress is lexical in Greek, in the sense that it is largely unpredictable by phonological criteria such as syllable weight or vowel quality, and dependent on lexical specification instead. ... There is one important observation on the lexical assignment of stress, in all categories of Greek words: it is restricted by a three-syllable window (at least in the standard language, which is discussed here). Stress can fall on any of the last three syllables, but not on any other syllable of the word.

new_statements.quote: This article investigates whether lexical frequency drives stress assignment in Greek, a morphology-dependent stress system. [...] Adults show systematic inflection-class conditioning: their stress patterns broadly follow the lexicon's dominant stress pattern per inflection class but depart from its distributional frequencies. Children exhibit a strong, frequency-insensitive preference for penultimate stress that persists across inflection classes, with only traces of suffix-specific stress preferences emerging in Grade 6. We argue that lexical frequency operates within grammatically imposed boundaries: the phonological default and inflection-class conditioning together determine the extent to which distributional patterns in the lexicon shape stress assignment.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Greek word stress is not phonologically predictable: it is a 'morphology-dependent' system in which the stress of a noun is conditioned by its inflection class (adults follow each class's dominant pattern) on top of a phonological default; children, before they have learned the class conditioning, put stress on the penult by default. The abstract does not state which syllable the adult phonological default is.
new_statements.exceptions: Children in Grades 3 and 6 show a frequency-insensitive penultimate preference across inflection classes; adults depart from lexical frequency distributions while following the dominant pattern per class.

new_statements.quote: Greek is a morphology-dependent stress system, where stress is lexically specified for a number of individual morphemes (e.g., roots and suffixes). In the absence of lexically encoded stress, a default stress emerges. Most theoretical analyses of Greek stress that assume antepenultimate stress to represent the default (e.g., Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1989; Ralli & Touratzidis 1992; Revithiadou 1999) are not independently confirmed by experimental studies [...] two production (reading aloud) experiments, which revealed, for our consultants, first, an almost complete lack of antepenultimate stress and, second, a split between penultimate and final stress dependent on acronym length, the type of the final segment and the syllable type of the penultimate syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically specified on individual morphemes (roots, suffixes), so it is not predictable from phonology; a default emerges only where no morpheme carries lexical stress. The theoretical antepenultimate default is not experimentally confirmed: in acronyms (no overt morphology) speakers almost never use antepenultimate stress, splitting instead between penultimate and final stress according to length, final segment (consonant-final acronyms take final stress) and penult syllable type; vowel-final acronyms tend to copy the stress of the inflected word they stand for; otherwise speakers prefer stress at stem edges.
new_statements.exceptions: Acronyms: consonant-final ones take end stress; vowel-final ones follow the inflected word they represent when enough morphonological information is available; antepenultimate stress is almost absent in acronyms.
new_statements.identity_note: All works concern Standard Modern Greek; none describes a particular dialect. Papangeli 2004 (indexes 5 and 6) is one dissertation listed twice by Glottolog (Dutch and English title forms).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Greek word stress is lexical: roots and suffixes may carry pre-assigned accents and a grammar-specific principle resolves conflicts (root accent beats the gen.pl. -ón accent: selíð-on vs melis-ón); when no morpheme is accented the phonological ('elsewhere') default is antepenultimate (mélisa). In acronyms, which lack inflection and lexical accent, speakers' productions almost never show antepenultimate stress: the 'dynamic default' is final stress for consonant-final and longer acronyms and penultimate/final for vowel-final ones depending on the inflected word the final vowel evokes, so the theoretical default and the speakers' preferred pattern do not coincide.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not discussed (single word stress; acronyms treated as single prosodic words)
new_statements.exceptions: Highly frequent lexicalised acronyms have fixed stress and may inflect (ðeí, oté, p. 190 fn. 4); place names, loanwords and brand names have fixed stress on a specific syllable (Ámsterdam, Gúcci, p. 191); Apoussidou (2011) is cited as claiming the Greek default is final (p. 189 fn. 3); pseudo-word experiments (Protopapas et al. 2006 etc.) favour penultimate stress in certain noun classes.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened works describe Standard Modern Greek (Athenian/standard variety; Revithiadou et al. 2015 consultants are AUTh students, Thessaloniki; Georgakopoulos & Skopeteas 2010 experimental Standard Modern Greek). Reed 2014 most likely concerns Ancient/Classical Greek (different glottocode) but this is unverified. Bibliographic correction for work 3: author Sylvia Reed alone, Bartolotta is the volume editor.

new_statements.quote: l’accent de mot en grec moderne est libre car d’une part, il existe dans cette langue des paires minimales différenciées uniquement par la place de l’accent, et d’autre part, certains morphèmes contraignent la place de l’accent ; cependant il est fixe car ceci n’est possible qu’à l’intérieur d’une " zone accentuable ". Selon Botinis (1989), cette zone est établie par la contrainte triconsonantique, sachant que l’accent ne peut se poser au delà de l’antépénultième syllabe du mot. [...] Enfin, l’accent de mot en grec moderne est considéré en général comme non prédictible, ce qui explique la présence de paires minimales qui se distinguent uniquement par la place de l’accent.
new_statements.translation: word accent in Modern Greek is free because, on the one hand, the language has minimal pairs distinguished only by the place of the accent and, on the other, certain morphemes constrain the place of the accent; yet it is fixed in that this is only possible inside an 'accentable zone'. According to Botinis (1989) this zone is set by the three-syllable constraint, the accent being unable to fall further back than the antepenultimate syllable of the word. [...] Finally, word accent in Modern Greek is generally considered unpredictable, which explains the existence of minimal pairs distinguished only by the place of the accent. (Preceding sentence, same page: 'In Garde's (1968) terms, Greek is a language with limited-freedom accent'.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Greek has a lexical (dynamic/intensity) word accent with no fixed position: it is given by the lexicon and by accent-affecting morphemes, may fall on any of the last three syllables (never further back than the antepenult, Botinis's three-syllable constraint, which also holds inside a constituent/clitic group), and is generally regarded as unpredictable, witness minimal pairs such as [çoros] 'dance' (final) vs 'place' (penult) and [spanjos] adverb (oxytone) vs adjective (paroxytone); Garde's label 'accent à liberté limitée'; p. 90: 'Le grec moderne est une langue à accent lexical.. qui n’a pas de place fixe dans le mot'; p. 23 (after Botinis): 'l’accent lexical, donné par le lexique, se situe n’importe où sur l’une des trois dernières syllabes'. Statistical near-predictability is noted: Tseva (1988) predicts the accent from word-final phonological structure in >80% of cases, the remaining 20% being sub-rules or exceptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §1.1.4 p. 92: when the stressed vowel is preceded by at least two unstressed vowels an accent appears on the second vowel to its left (Jacob & Philippaki: secondary accent; Nespor & Vogel 1986, 1989 call it the primary and the word accent secondary; Yoo: a rhythmic accent); with enclitics a 'syntagmatic' accent (Botinis) appears on the second syllable to the right of the word accent, the three-syllable law applying to the word+clitic group. Acoustically (§1.1.2 and the Ch. 3 experiments) stressed vowels are longer, higher and more intense than unstressed ones in neutral intonation.
new_statements.exceptions: Minimal pairs by accent place are 'peu nombreuses'; accent shifts due to morphology/derivation are explicitly set aside (refers to Tseva & Contini 1988, Tsitsopoulos 1973); Tseva's statistical rules leave ~20% sub-rules/exceptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Modern Greek (Athens); the experimental chapters use read speech by native speakers of standard Greek; Ancient Greek pitch accent is mentioned only historically (§1.1.2).

new_statements.quote: It is generally agreed that Greek words carry only one stress, on one of their last three syllables (among many, Setatos 1974, Householder et al. 1964, Warburton 1970a, Joseph & Warburton 1987, Holton et al. 1997). The position of stress is largely determined by morphology and is phonologically unpredictable, though some patterns are more frequent than others (Revithiadou 1998, 1999). Compared to languages like English, stress in Greek bears a significant amount of functional load, in that there are several pairs and even triplets of words distinguished solely by stress location, as in [xaˈmoʝela] “smiles, n.”, [xamoˈʝela] “smile, imper.”, [xamoʝeˈla] “s/he smiles”.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each Greek (content) word has exactly one lexical stress, which must fall on one of the last three syllables (the 'trisyllabic' window); within that window its position is set by morphology/lexicon and is not predictable from phonological shape (no weight or vowel-quality conditioning), so stress is contrastive (minimal pairs and triplets by stress position alone). Most polysyllabic function words are stressless in speech regardless of orthographic accent.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Greek primary word stress is confined to the last three syllables of the word (rightmost foot strongest) but its position within that window is lexically determined: stems and many derivational/inflectional suffixes carry inherent stress properties, and minimal pairs like nómos/nomós, pérno/pernó show stem stress is not predictable by rule. Inherently stressed suffixes override stem stress. In [stem+stem] compounds (and prefix+stem words) with no inherently stressed suffix, a compound stress rule assigns antepenultimate stress regardless of the members' own stresses (kuklóspito < kúkla + spíti); [stem+word] compounds keep the stress of the second member (stress preservation); [word+word] (phrasal) compounds keep both word stresses, the rightmost being strongest at the phrase level.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Type-1/2 compounds and long noncompound words may carry a rhythmic secondary stress to the left of the primary (e.g. on the first syllable of màvrovúni, sòfrosíni), its location governed by rhythmic alternation and 'characterized by a certain degree of optionality'; fn. 8 notes Arvaniti (1992) found no acoustic evidence for rhythmic stress in Greek. Fn. 8 also reports the enclitic-stress dispute (host + clitics adding a stress to the right of the lexical stress; which of the two is stronger varies, by the authors' observation, with speaker generation).
new_statements.exceptions: Neuters in -i ([stem+stem] spirtokúti etc.) show penultimate rather than antepenultimate stress, handled by positing a zero inflectional syllable slot (no Greek neuter in -i has antepenultimate stress); exocentric compounds in -is (anixtoxéris) take penultimate stress because that ending requires stress on the preceding syllable; stem+pseudostem compounds (astronómos, tavromáxos) keep the pseudostem's inherent stress; loanword second members (tavérna, saláta, petséta) preserve their original stress; parasynthetic formations (ksekárfotos) escape suffix stress.

readall_conflicts: On the type of system there is no disagreement: the two abstracts I could read (Revithiadou, Nikolou & Papadopoulou 2015; Revithiadou et al. 2026) both call Greek a morphology-dependent stress system in which stress is lexically specified on morphemes, which is the catalog's lexical coding and van Oostendorp's (2012) statement. They disagree with the existing statement on the default: van Oostendorp says antepenultimate stress is the default, whereas the 2015 abstract states that the antepenultimate default assumed by Malikouti-Drachman & Drachman 1989, Ralli & Touratzidis 1992 and Revithiadou 1999 'is not independently confirmed by experimental studies' and that acronyms show 'an almost complete lack of antepenultimate stress', splitting between penultimate and final stress; the 2026 abstract adds that children default to penultimate stress across inflection classes. Neither abstract states the adult phonological default syllable, so the default remains contested rather than settled; the acronym result is domain-specific (morphology-free words) and the child result is developmental.

sources.quote: This article investigates whether lexical frequency drives stress assignment in Greek, a morphology-dependent stress system. [...] Adults show systematic inflection-class conditioning: their stress patterns broadly follow the lexicon's dominant stress pattern per inflection class but depart from its distributional frequencies. Children exhibit a strong, frequency-insensitive preference for penultimate stress that persists across inflection classes, with only traces of suffix-specific stress preferences emerging in Grade 6. We argue that lexical frequency operates within grammatically imposed boundaries: the phonological default and inflection-class conditioning together determine the extent to which distributional patterns in the lexicon shape stress assignment.

sources.quote: Greek is a morphology-dependent stress system, where stress is lexically specified for a number of individual morphemes (e.g., roots and suffixes). sources.quote: It is generally agreed that Greek words carry only one stress, on one of their last three syllables (among many, Setatos 1974, Householder et al. 1964, Warburton 1970a, Joseph & Warburton 1987, Holton et al. 1997). The position of stress is largely determined by morphology and is phonologically unpredictable, though some patterns are more frequent than others (Revithiadou 1998, 1999). Compared to languages like English, stress in Greek bears a significant amount of functional load, in that there are several pairs and even triplets of words distinguished solely by stress location, as in [xaˈmoʝela] “smiles, n.”, [xamoˈʝela] “smile, imper.”, [xamoʝeˈla] “s/he smiles”.

sources.quote: Greek is a language with “dynamic” stress.
